title: Modeling the Nephron
question: How do filtration, recovery and secretion change the fluid that becomes urine?

blocks.prompt: Required before observing: Predict whether both useful glucose and waste urea could enter the first filtrate. Will that filtrate have the same makeup as final urine? Explain your reasons.
blocks.text: I predict that glucose and urea can both enter filtrate, with later recovery and secretion changing final urine. A filter may separate by barrier properties rather than deciding what is useful.

blocks.prompt: Required before observing: How could tracking a substance before filtering, after recovery and after secretion help explain its final amount? Why would repeating the same model three times add little evidence about real variation?
blocks.text: Track each substance separately through the same model. Units are chosen and different between substances; never add rows or infer human concentrations. Different directions/regions add evidence, not three duplicate trials.

blocks.prompt: No glucose units remain in final model urine. What explains this?
blocks.text:
Glucose entered the filtrate, then was recovered to blood.
Correct! The glucose marker passed the first filter. Proximal-tubule transport returned the modeled glucose to blood, rather than proving it never entered the filtrate. Revised after feedback.

blocks.prompt: Which direction describes the potassium secretion example?
blocks.text:
From blood through a late-tubule cell into the tubule fluid.
Correct! Secretion adds material to tubule fluid. Reabsorption returns material to blood; excretion carries final material away in urine. Correct on first recorded check.

blocks.prompt: Must every filtered urea unit remain in urine, and must these amounts fit every person?
blocks.text:
No. Some urea can be recovered/recycled; these amounts are chosen model bookkeeping.
Correct! Urea transport is more complex than a one-way waste pipe. Keep this chosen net recovery and the separate unit scales distinct from human concentrations. Correct on first recorded check.

Marker sizes, colors and counts are explanatory. Counts use a separate arbitrary scale for each substance; do not turn them into urine percentages, concentrations or human filtration/recovery rates. All amounts are chosen for bookkeeping. Pressure drives filtration; the filter does not recognize only waste. Cells and this large-protein marker stay in blood, but real small proteins can be filtered and recovered. The glucose trace shows a net proximal-tubule route through cells, tissue fluid and capillaries; sodium-linked carriers and supporting pumps are supplied details. Other water, urea and potassium recovery is supplied across the nephron, not all at that glucose site. Potassium secretion is one regulated late-tubule example, not an unchanging rule for every person. Urea can move in both directions and recycle; the model only gives a chosen net recovery. Hormones(chemical messages), detailed transport/energy steps, acid–base balance, many solutes and changing flow are omitted. Final urine goes through collecting passages to the ureter; filtrate does not go straight from the glomerulus to the bladder. One ideal model cannot show human variation, diagnose kidney function or predict treatment.
